triage.modern_statement: This fragment comes at the end of a list of tasks about Riemann surfaces, so the exact question is partly cut off. It names two things. (a) Given a (closed) Riemann surface, find and describe its finite-sheeted unbranched covering surfaces (2-fold, 3-fold, …). In modern terms these are its finite unramified covers, which correspond to finite-index subgroups of the fundamental group. (b) The uniformisation problem: map the universal covering surface conformally onto a standard domain, such as the interior of the unit disk (or the plane or the sphere). Equivalently, write an algebraic or analytic curve using single-valued automorphic functions. This is the uniformisation theorem for Riemann surfaces.
triage.answered_by: The uniformisation part is essentially Hilbert's 22nd Problem (1900), uniformising analytic relations by automorphic functions. Poincaré and Koebe solved it independently in 1907: Poincaré's memoir appeared in early November 1907, and Koebe published proofs in 1907, including a simplified version of Poincaré's proof at the end of November. The unbranched-covering part follows from the covering-space theory developed by Schwarz and others, and is standard today; I did not find a separate source tied to this note.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 22nd problem, from his 1900 list, asks for the uniformisation of analytic relations by means of automorphic functions.

Poincaré's memoir proving the general uniformisation theorem appeared in early November 1907. At the end of November 1907 Koebe published a simplified version of Poincaré's proof, so by the end of 1907 the theorem was firmly established. Both relate this to Hilbert's 22nd problem.

Covering-space theory, which Schwarz developed specifically to study the uniformisation problem, links uniformisation to conformal mapping of Riemann surfaces. Koebe and Poincaré proved the uniformisation theorem in 1907.

Third, higher-dimensional and related versions of the 22nd problem are still studied, but the one-variable version mentioned here is settled.
